Finding: Food waste is commercially material in UK hospitality and food service.
Evidence basis: 1.1m tonnes HaFS food waste; £3.2bn sector cost; ~£10k/outlet average.
Interpretation: There is a real prevention problem, but FreshRoute cannot claim that all waste is logistics-caused.
Business-plan decision: Position waste reduction as a potential co-benefit; measure it as a pilot KPI rather than forecast a fixed saving.
Caution: Avoid attributing sector-average waste directly to Coventry SMEs.

Finding: Coventry provides a large screening universe but not an evidenced numeric SAM.
Evidence basis: FSA lists 3,015 food businesses on the 17 Sep 2026 release; business type, independence and supplier patterns require further screening.
Interpretation: The opportunity cannot be justified by the headline count alone.
Business-plan decision: Use FSA business types plus independence, chilled-flow, supplier and geography qualification; do not manufacture an eligibility percentage.
Caution: No current secondary source establishes the number willing/able to use FreshRoute.

Finding: Food-logistics compliance extends beyond the 8°C rule.
Evidence basis: FSA registration guidance plus Regulation 852/2004 transport controls and chilled-food guidance.
Interpretation: Registration/FBO status, hygiene, separation, traceability, custody and temperature monitoring are launch conditions.
Business-plan decision: G0 requires written responsibility/registration confirmation and contracted transport controls.
Caution: Exact responsibility depends on the final contractual architecture.

Finding: Collaboration benefits depend on relational and information mechanisms.
Evidence basis: Stoeva et al. (2024); Badraoui et al. (2022); Relational View.
Interpretation: Pooling is not only route optimisation; common information routines and governance affect whether value is realised.
Business-plan decision: Use minimum data standards, clear custody/cost allocation and common route routines.
Caution: Much empirical evidence is not UK micro-foodservice-specific.

Finding: Time capacity is feasible in the base route, but payload and receiving windows remain constraints.
Evidence basis: 4 pickups + 12 SME drops ≈6.35h; 14-drop stretch ≈7.02h; 16 drops ≈8.0h. Refrigerated L2 payload benchmark 801-1000kg.
Interpretation: The binding constraint can shift from time to payload or simultaneous customer receiving windows.
Business-plan decision: Use 14 drops as a planning ceiling only; validate order weight and receiving windows at G1/G3.
Caution: Stop times, order weights and actual Coventry routing are scenario inputs.

Finding: Freshness should be an eligibility constraint, not an assumed benefit.
Interpretation: More consolidation is not automatically better for short-shelf-life goods.
Business-plan decision: Each product class needs supplier-defined remaining-life / route-dwell eligibility rules.
Caution: No universal shelf-life threshold is assumed.

Finding: Incumbents and substitutes make a broad delivery proposition unattractive.
Evidence basis: Booker, Bidfood, Brakes, supplier delivery, vehicle hire and SME self-collection.
Interpretation: FreshRoute only adds value where businesses intentionally retain multiple local/specialist suppliers.
Business-plan decision: Position as supplier-neutral coordination, not generic wholesaling or van hire.
Caution: Company sources describe observable propositions, not independent performance.

Finding: The current £25/drop price is a threshold case, not robust scale economics.
Evidence basis: At £275 contracted route-day cost and 21 active SMEs, EBITDA margin is only about 1%; 15% margin requires ~£29.8/drop.
Interpretation: Positive EBITDA alone is not sufficient to justify scale.
Business-plan decision: Treat >=10% margin as a minimum scale gate; validate price and contracted route cost before launch.
Caution: £275 route cost and £25/£30 prices remain scenarios until commercially quoted/tested.

Finding: The outsourced 3PL architecture must be costed as outsourced transport.
Evidence basis: Internal consistency audit of operating architecture and financial model.
Interpretation: A self-drive van + FreshRoute driver cost build cannot be used as the principal cost if the business buys a 3PL route.
Business-plan decision: Use contracted 3PL cost envelope; retain £214.66 self-operated figure only as a comparator.

Finding: Customer value must be compared with the economic burden of fragmented collection.
Evidence basis: Scenario: 1-2 hours of staff/owner time plus 10-30 miles at £12.71/h and 55p/mile gives ~£18-£42.
Interpretation: The £25 drop fee may be rational where it replaces a sufficiently costly fragmented trip, but willingness to pay is not observed.
Business-plan decision: Use the comparator only to structure G1 commercial validation.
Caution: Mileage/time scenarios are not customer research.
